title: Polls close in less than an hour as British Columbians choose next provincial government

image.caption: The Greens' watch party in Central Saanich tonight. (Emily Fagan/CBC)

items: October 25Green supporters optimistic ahead of polls closingThe Greens' watch party in Central Saanich tonight. (Emily Fagan/CBC)I'm at Church and State Winery in Central Saanich where about 100 B.C. Green Party supporters are gathered. There's a bubbling excitement in the room as people enter, grabbing snacks from a charcuterie board and posing in a photo booth.

Gunn, Merrifield in attendance at B.C. Conservative watch partyTarnjit ParmarSupporters at the B.C. Conservative election night watch party tonight. (Tarnjit Parmar/CBC)I’m a producer with CBC News at the B.C. Conservative Party election night watch party at Rocky Mountaineer Station in Vancouver. Doors have opened and supporters are pouring into the venue. Aaron Gunn, the federal Conservative MP for North Island-Powell River is in attendance as is Katy Merrifield, campaign director for the B.C. Conservatives. Merrifield faced criticism over anti-Islam posts shared on social media earlier this year. Sam Sullivan, the former mayor of Vancouver and two-time MLA under the B.C. Liberals, has also made an appearance. A number of former staffers from the B.C. Liberals tell us they are happy to be here tonight to offer their support to B.C. Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson. We are being told that around 1,300 people will be here tonight, as results roll in from around the province after polls close at 8 p.m. PT.

NDP headquarters are quiet as the clock ticks downNadia JannifThe NDP headquarters in Vancouver. (Nadia Jannif/CBC)I'm working alongside provincial affairs reporter Katie DeRosa tonight at B.C. NDP headquarters in downtown Vancouver. The room is lit up and ready, but mostly empty as various media outlets prepare for election results to come in. Polls close in less than 10 minutes.

U.S. trade dispute, bid for stronger majority among Eby's reasons for election callRhianna SchmunkEby calls snap B.C. election citing 'existential' Trump threatB.C. NDP Leader David Eby called an early provincial election to be held on Oct. 24, citing the 'existential' threat of U.S. President Donald Trump's trade war on Canada. Eby also dismissed questions about the ethics of calling the vote while the B.C. Conservative Party is in disarray.When Eby called the early provincial election, he presented the vote as British Columbians' chance to choose which government will meet the "existential" threat posed by the trade dispute between Canada and the United States. But he distanced himself from that rationale as the campaign progressed, making no mention of the Trump administration or the U.S. president's name in response to a question about his snap election decision during the leaders' debate on Oct. 14.Eby has also said his party needs a stronger majority, with its current one-seat margin preventing his government from doing "what needs to be done" because it was too fragile — citing the need for every party MLA to vote every time to ensure its legislation is passed. He said another election couldn't wait even a few weeks until after last week's local elections because he believed the political landscape has changed so dramatically since his government was elected two years ago.Candidates from opposing political parties criticized the early election as "cynical," though they have welcomed an opportunity for change in Victoria after nine years of NDP rule.

The B.C. NDP's platformAkshay KulkarniDavid Eby makes the case for another 4 yearsDavid Eby is asking British Columbians for another four years as premier. But after calling a snap election with the opposition party in chaos, the NDP is now facing a serious challenge from the B.C. Conservatives. The CBC's Katie DeRosa looks at Eby's promises, setbacks, and the political gamble that will determine his future.The NDP's platform is largely built on continuing the work it's done over its past nine years in power — particularly by boosting health-care recruitment from the U.S and reducing the province's reliance on its southern neighbour through major projects. The party's platform predicts the province's deficit will fall by $2 billion over two years, according to its costing, some of which is predicated on income tax increases for the top 3.88 per cent of earners in B.C.The NDP is also promising to freeze auto insurance rates for three years; a temporary 10 per cent reduction of the provincial fuel tax; and an expansion of vacancy and speculation taxes to increase housing development.

Unknown factor could be an asset for Doerkson and the ConservativesKatie DeRosaDoerkson during a campaign stop in Sidney, B.C., on Tuesday. (Chad Hipolito/The Canadian Press)Doerkson is the first person to admit he did not set out to become the leader of the B.C. Conservative Party. "Of course, it was a little bit of a short notice," Doerkson told CBC News earlier this month from his home in Williams Lake, B.C., in his signature understated tone.While people across the political spectrum describe Doerkson, 58, as a nice guy, he's an unelected and largely unknown party leader who has been finding his feet in the election campaign. Andrew Reeve, a former B.C. Liberal communications director who worked alongside Doerkson in that caucus, said that could be a source of strength for the two-term MLA."There's that old adage of perhaps we should give power to those who don't seek it, and I think that really fits the type of guy that Lorne is," Reeve told me earlier this month. "The person that'll lend you their truck or they'll give you a ride home from the airport."

The B.C. Conservatives' platformAkshay KulkarniUnexpected leader: Lorne Doerkson pitches himself to British ColumbiansB.C. Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson finds himself in an unprecedented situation. Doerkson is set to make his main pitch to British Columbians on the debate stage Wednesday night. Katie DeRosa caught up with Doerkson at his home in Williams Lake.While the Conservatives were in disarray little more than a month ago — facing a number of splinter parties and an unpopular leader — when the snap election was called they quickly coalesced around Doerkson, who initially assumed his role on an interim basis. The party's platform has focused on attacking the NDP's near-decade in office and promising to rein in the province's deficit. According to the Conservatives' platform, if they are elected the province's deficit would fall to $10.8 billion by 2030, with the party promising to freeze outside hiring, cut consultants and review spending across ministries to find billions in savings.The party has promised to complete the new Surrey Hospital and B.C. Cancer Centre, and build a new women's and children's hospital in Surrey. It has pledged to expand detox and treatment services, along with ending the safe supply of drugs, to deal with the toxic drug crisis.In addition, the Conservatives have promised to replace the George Massey Tunnel in Delta with a 10-lane bridge, largely scrap the province's no-fault auto insurance model and repeal the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act.

Green leader aims to hold the balance of powerEmily FaganLowan during the B.C. election provincial leaders’ debate in Vancouver on Oct. 14. (Ethan Cairns/CBC)Last year, in a campaign that echoed the style of Zohran Mamdani's push to become New York mayor, Lowan became one of the youngest people elected to lead a political party in Canada.Without a seat in the legislature — of which the Greens held two — she's spent much of the past year touring the province to build grassroots support.Lowan, 26, hopes to win the balance of power in Victoria — but first, needs to win herself a seat. She's running in Saanich North and the Islands, a riding formerly held by the Greens' Rob Botterell."I think my ask to voters is, I'm not going to be premier in a week, but I do want the B.C. Greens to hold a minority government to account," she told CBC News.The Greens will have "terms and conditions" for any party they work with, she says, and did not rule out striking a deal with the B.C. Conservatives to form government."Nothing's off the table," she said.Lowan says over its nine years in power, the NDP has broken trust with First Nations, abandoned climate promises and let affordability challenges spiral.

The B.C. Greens' platformAkshay KulkarniLowan in North Saanich, B.C., on Thursday. (Chad Hipolito/The Canadian Press)The B.C. Green Party entered the snap election campaign with their leader not having a seat in the legislature — and Lowan has argued that voters should send Green MLAs to Victoria to keep the other two major parties in check, ideally through a minority government.Lowan's party is critical of both the NDP's record in office and the Conservatives' positions on key issues.Its platform has pledged a windfall tax on mega-corporations and making B.C.'s richest people pay more — with a proposed "Fair Share Act" predicted to raise $22.2 billion in its first year and $5.4 billion every year thereafter — and promises to expand union jobs in areas like renewable energy.The Greens have promised to lift the NDP's freeze on new $10-a-day child-care spaces, and pledged that every British Columbian would have free and universal child care by 2031. The party's platform includes promises of free transit; an expansion of community health centres; expanding non-market housing along with vacancy control; and boosting harm-reduction measures to deal with the toxic drug crisis.

CentreBC's platformAkshay KulkarniCentreBC Leader Elenore Sturko has said her fledgling party aims to give a voice to those feeling politically homeless. (Hunter Soo/CBC)CentreBC Leader Elenore Sturko was one of many former B.C. Conservative MLAs that joined the fledgling party amid chaos in the Tories' caucus. But she ended up being the lone high-profile MLA left standing after many CentreBC members rejoined the Conservatives under Doerkson.Sturko has told CBC News that her party wants to provide a home for centrist voters who feel alienated by both the Conservatives and the NDP, saying CentreBC has fiscally responsible, socially progressive policies.The party has pledged to push for hiring hundreds more provincial RCMP officers if its candidates are elected, along with increasing the renter's tax credit and providing more seats in schools.
